title: 11  Ideal and Non-Ideal Gases
text:
11.4 Fugacity
The chemical potential of a pure ideal gas can be calculated using eq. 9.21. Since we are not interested in a mixture, we can drop the asterisk in \(\mu^*\), and rewrite eq. 9.21 as:
\[
\mu_{\text{ideal}} = \mu^\standardstate + RT \ln \frac{P}{P^\standardstate}.
\tag{11.28}\]
For a non-ideal gas, the pressure cannot be used in eq. 11.28 because the response of each gas to changes in pressure is not universal. We can, however, define a new variable to replace the pressure in eq. 11.28 and call it fugacity (\(f\)).

Definition 11.3 Fugacity: The effective pressure of a non-ideal gas that corresponds to the pressure of an ideal gas with the same temperature and chemical potential of the non-ideal one.

Eq. 11.28 then becomes:
\[
\mu_{\text{non-ideal}} = \mu^\standardstate + RT \ln \frac{f}{P^\standardstate}.
\tag{11.29}\]
Since the chemical potential of a gas \(\mu\) is equal to the standard chemical potential \(\mu^\standardstate\) when \(P=P^\standardstate\), it is easy to use eq. 11.29 to demonstrate that:
\[
\lim_{P\rightarrow 0} \frac{f}{P} = 1,
\tag{11.30}\]
in other words, any non-ideal gas will approach the ideal gas behavior as \(P\rightarrow 0\). This condition, in conjunction with the \(T\rightarrow \infty\) behavior obtained in the previous section, results in the following statement:

The highest chances for any gas to behave ideally happen at high temperature and low pressure.

We can now return our attention to the definition of fugacity. Remembering that the chemical potential is the molar Gibbs energy of a substance, we can write:
\[
d \mu_{\text{ideal}} = \overline{V}_{\text{ideal}}dP,
\tag{11.31}\]
and:
\[
d \mu_{\text{non-ideal}} = \overline{V}_{\text{non-ideal}}dP.
\tag{11.32}\]
Subtracting eq. 11.31 from eq. 11.32, we obtain:
\[
d \mu_{\text{non-ideal}}-d \mu_{\text{ideal}} = \left(\overline{V}_{\text{non-ideal}}-\overline{V}_{\text{ideal}} \right) dP,
\tag{11.33}\]
which we can then integrate between \(0\) and \(P\):
\[
\mu_{\text{non-ideal}}-\mu_{\text{ideal}} = \int_0^P \left(\overline{V}_{\text{non-ideal}}-\overline{V}_{\text{ideal}} \right) dP.
\tag{11.34}\]
Using eq. 11.28 and eq. 11.29 we can then replace the definition of chemical potentials, resulting in:
\[
\ln f - \ln P = \frac{1}{RT} \int_0^P \left(\overline{V}_{\text{non-ideal}} - \overline{V}_{\text{ideal}} \right) dP,
\tag{11.35}\]
which gives us a mathematical definition of the fugacity, as:
\[
f = P \cdot \underbrace{\exp\left[ \frac{1}{RT} \int_0^P \left(\overline{V}_{\text{non-ideal}}-\overline{V}_{\text{ideal}} \right) dP \right]}_{\text{fugacity coefficient, }\phi(T,P)}.
\tag{11.36}\]
The exponential term in eq. 11.36 is complicated to write, but it can be interpreted as a coefficient—unique to each non-ideal gas—that can be measured experimentally. Such coefficients are dependent on pressure and temperature and are called the fugacity coefficients. Using letter \(\phi\) to represent the fugacity coefficient, we can rewrite eq. 11.36 as:
\[
f = \phi P,
\tag{11.37}\]
which gives us a straightforward interpretation of the fugacity as an effective pressure. As such, the fugacity will have the same unit as the pressure, while the fugacity coefficients will be dimensionless.
As we already saw in chapter 10, the fugacity can be used to replace the pressure in the definition of the equilibrium constant for reactions that involve non-ideal gases. The new constant is usually called \(K_f\), and is obtained from:
\[
K_f=\prod_i f_{i,\text{eq}}^{\nu_i} = K_P \prod_i \phi_{i}^{\nu_i}.
\tag{11.38}\]

11.5 Chapter Review

11.5.1 Practice Problems
Problem 1: Calculating the van der Waals Constants
A gas has a critical temperature of \(400\,\text{K}\) and critical pressure of \(80\,\text{bar}\). Calculate its van der Waals constants \(a\) and \(b\).
Solution: Consider the first two formulas in eq. 11.26:
\[T_c = \frac{8a}{27Rb},\]
\[P_c = \frac{a}{27b^2}.\]
We can rearrange the equation for the critical pressure, to get:
\[a = 27b^2P_c,\]
then replace this into the equation for the critical temperature:
\[T_c = \frac{8(27b^2P_c)}{27Rb} = \frac{8bP_c}{R},\]
Given:
\(T_c = 400\,\text{K}\),
\(P_c = 80.0\,\text{bar}\),
\(R = 0.083145\,\frac{\text{L}\,\text{bar}}{\text{mol}\,\text{K}}\).
We can now solve for \(b\):
\[b = \frac{RT_c}{8P_c} = \frac{0.083145 \cdot 400}{8 \cdot 80} = 0.0519\,\text{L}/\text{mol}.\]
Now we can calculate \(a\):
\[a = 27b^2P_c = 27 \cdot (0.0519)^2 \cdot 80 = 5.82\,\text{L}^2\cdot\text{bar}/\text{mol}^2\]
Answer: The van der Waals constants for the given gas are: \(a = 5.82\,\text{L}^2\cdot\text{bar}/\text{mol}^2\) \(b = 0.0519\,\text{L}/\text{mol}\)

Problem 2: Determining the Joule-Thomson Coefficient
Calculate the Joule-Thomson coefficient for a gas with \(C_P = 30\,\frac{\text{J}}{\text{mol}\,\text{K}}\) and \(\left(\frac{\partial H}{\partial P}\right)_T = -0.02\,\frac{\text{J}}{\text{mol}\,\text{bar}}\) at \(300\,\text{K}\) and \(1.0\,\text{bar}\).
Solution: The Joule-Thomson coefficient is defined in eq. 11.22 as:
\[\mu_{JT} = \left(\frac{\partial T}{\partial P}\right)_H = -\frac{1}{C_P}\left(\frac{\partial H}{\partial P}\right)_T.\]
Given:
\(C_P = 30\,\frac{\text{J}}{\text{mol}\,\text{K}}\),
\(\left(\frac{\partial H}{\partial P}\right)_T = -0.02\,\frac{\text{J}}{\text{mol}\,\text{bar}}\),
\(T = 300\,\text{K}\),
\(P = 1.0\,\text{bar}\).
Then:
\[\mu_{JT} = -\frac{1}{30\,\frac{\text{J}}{\text{mol}\,\text{K}}} \cdot \left(-0.02\,\frac{\text{J}}{\text{mol}\,\text{bar}}\right) = 6.667 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{K}/\text{bar}\]
Adjusting the significant digits gives us the final answer.
Answer: The Joule-Thomson coefficient for the gas is \(6.7 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{K}/\text{bar}\)

Problem 3: Calculating the Boyle Temperature
Calculate the Boyle temperature for a gas with van der Waals constants \(a = 3.5\,\text{L}^2\cdot\text{bar}/\text{mol}^2\) and \(b = 0.04\,\text{L}/\text{mol}\).
Solution: The Boyle temperature is defined as:
\[T_B = \frac{a}{bR}.\]
Given:
\(a = 3.5\,\text{L}^2\cdot\text{bar}/\text{mol}^2\),
\(b = 0.04\,\text{L}/\text{mol}\),
\(R = 0.083145\,\frac{\text{L}\,\text{bar}}{\text{mol}\,\text{K}}\).
Then:
\[T_B = \frac{3.5\,\text{L}^2\cdot\text{bar}/\text{mol}^2}{0.04\,\text{L}/\text{mol} \cdot 0.083145\,\text{L}\cdot\text{bar}/\text{mol}\cdot\text{K}}=1052\,\text{K}\]
Answer: The Boyle temperature for the gas is \(1052\,\text{K}\)

Problem 4: Determining the Critical Compressibility Factor
A gas has a critical temperature of \(350\,\text{K}\), critical pressure of \(70\,\text{bar}\), and critical volume of \(0.15\,\text{L}/\text{mol}\). Calculate its critical compressibility factor.
Solution: The critical compressibility factor is given by eq. 11.27 as:
\[z_c = \frac{P_cV_c}{RT_c}\]
Given: \(T_c = 350\,\text{K}\),
\(P_c = 70\,\text{bar}\),
\(V_c = 0.15\,\text{L}/\text{mol}\),
\(R = 0.083145\,\frac{\text{L}\,\text{bar}}{\text{mol}\,\text{K}}\).
Then:
\[z_c = \frac{70\,\text{bar} \cdot 0.15\,\text{L}/\text{mol}}{0.083145\,\text{L}\cdot\text{bar}/\text{mol}\cdot\text{K} \cdot 350\,\text{K}}=0.361\]
Adjusting the significant digits gives us the final answer.
Answer: The critical compressibility factor for the gas is \(0.36\)

Problem 5: Calculating Fugacity
A gas at \(300\,\text{K}\) and \(50\,\text{bar}\) has a fugacity coefficient of 0.95. Calculate its fugacity.
Solution: The fugacity is defined in eq. 11.37 as:
\[f = \phi P\]
Given:
\(T = 300\,\text{K}\),
\(P = 50\,\text{bar}\),
\(\phi = 0.95\).
Then:
\[f = 0.95 \cdot 50\,\text{bar}=47.5\,\text{bar} \]
Adjusting the significant digits gives us the final answer.
Answer: The fugacity of the gas is \(48\,\text{bar}\)


11.5.2 Study Questions
1. Which of the following is NOT an assumption of the ideal gas model?

The particles occupy no volume.
The particles do not interact with each other.
The particles have no kinetic energy.
The particles are in constant motion.
The particles undergo perfectly elastic collisions.


2. What does the Joule-Thomson coefficient measure?

The rate of change of volume with respect to temperature.
The rate of change of pressure with respect to volume.
The rate of change of temperature with respect to pressure at constant enthalpy.
The rate of change of entropy with respect to temperature.
The rate of change of enthalpy with respect to pressure.


3. What is the value of the critical compressibility factor predicted by the van der Waals equation?

\(1/3\).
\(3/8\).
\(1/2\).
\(2/3\).
\(1/4\).


4. Which of the following statements about fugacity is correct?

Fugacity has units of pressure squared.
The fugacity coefficient is always greater than 1.
As pressure approaches zero, the ratio of fugacity to pressure approaches infinity.
Fugacity is independent of temperature for all gases.
Fugacity is used to replace pressure in equilibrium constant calculations for non-ideal gases.


5. How is the critical temperature of a gas defined?

The temperature at which the gas becomes a supercritical fluid.
The temperature above which the gas cannot be liquefied by pressure alone.
The temperature at which the gas occupies its largest volume.
The temperature at which the gas behaves most ideally.
The temperature at which the gas has zero compressibility.


6. The compressibility factor \(z\) for an ideal gas is always:

Greater than 1.
Less than 1.
Equal to 0.
Equal to 1.
Dependent on pressure.


7. How is the Boyle temperature defined?

The temperature at which a gas liquefies.
The temperature at which a gas behaves most ideally over a large pressure range.
The critical temperature of a gas.
The temperature at which a gas solidifies.
The temperature at which a gas has maximum entropy.


8. In the van der Waals equation, what does the parameter ‘\(a\)’ account for?

The volume of gas molecules.
The pressure of the gas.
The temperature of the gas.
The number of moles of the gas.
The intermolecular forces between gas molecules.


9. Which of the following is true regarding the fugacity of a gas?

It is always greater than its pressure.
It is always less than its pressure.
It is the effective pressure that corresponds to the chemical potential of the real gas.
It is independent of temperature.
It is only applicable to ideal gases.


10. Which of the following gases is likely to have a Joule-Thomson inversion temperature below room temperature?

Nitrogen.
Oxygen.
Carbon dioxide.
Helium.
Water vapor.








TipAnswers





1.c, 2.c, 3.b, 4.e, 5.b, 6.d, 7.b, 8.e, 9.c, 10.d

title: 12  Phase Equilibrium
text:
12.1 Phase Stability
We have already encountered the gas, liquid, and solid phases and already discussed some of their properties. These terms are intuitive since these are the three most common states of matter.1 For this reason, we have previously used the terms without the necessity of formally defining their meaning. However, a formal definition of “phase” is necessary to discuss several concepts in this chapter and the following ones:
Let’s now use the total differential of the chemical potential and the definition of molar Gibbs energy for one component:
\[
\begin{aligned}
d\mu &= \left( \frac{\partial \mu}{\partial T} \right)_P dT + \left( \frac{\partial \mu}{\partial P} \right)_T dP \\
d\mu &= -SdT+\overline{V}dP,
\end{aligned}
\tag{12.1}\]
to write:
\[
\left( \frac{\partial \mu}{\partial T} \right)_P=-S \qquad \left( \frac{\partial \mu}{\partial P} \right)_T =\overline{V}.
\tag{12.2}\]
We can use these definitions to study the dependence of the chemical potential with respect to changes in pressure and temperature. If we plot \(\mu\) as a function of \(T\) using the first coefficient in eq. 12.2, we obtain the diagram in Figure 12.1. The diagram presents three curves, each corresponding to one of the three most common states of matter – solid, liquid, and gas. As we saw in several previous chapters, the entropy of a phase is almost constant with respect to temperature,2 and therefore the three curves are essentially straight, with negative angular coefficients \(-S\). This also explains why the solid phase has a basically flat line since, according to the third law, the entropy of a perfect solid is zero and close to zero if the solid is not perfect. The difference between the three lines’ angular coefficients is explained by the fact that each of these states has a different value of entropy:
\[
\left( \frac{\partial \mu_{\text{solid}}}{\partial T} \right)_P =-S_{\text{s}} \qquad \left( \frac{\partial \mu_{\text{liquid}}}{\partial T} \right)_P =-S_{\text{l}} \qquad \left( \frac{\partial \mu_{\text{gas}}}{\partial T} \right)_P =-S_{\text{g}},
\tag{12.3}\]
and since the entropy of a gas is always bigger than the entropy of a liquid, which in turn, is yet bigger than the entropy of a solid (\(S_{\text{g}} \gg S_{\text{l}}>S_{\text{s}}\)), we obtain three lines with different angular coefficients that intersect each other. At each temperature, the phase with the lowest chemical potential will be the most stable (see red segments in Figure 12.1). At each intersection between two lines, the two phases have the same chemical potential, representing the temperature at which they coexist. This temperature is the temperature at which the phase change happens. Recalling from general chemistry, at the junction between the solid and the liquid lines, the fusion (fus) process occurs, and the corresponding temperature is called the melting point \(T_{\text{m}}\). At the junction between the liquid and the gas lines, the vaporization (vap) process happens, and the corresponding temperature is called the boiling point \(T_{\text{b}}\). Depending on the substance and the pressure at which the process happens, the solid line might intersect the gas line before the liquid line. When that occurs, the liquid phase is never observed, and only the sublimation (subl) process happens at the sublimation point \(T_{\text{subl}}\).
The effects of pressure on this diagram can be studied using the second coefficient in eq. 12.2. For the majority of substances, \(\overline{V}_{\text{g}} \gg \overline{V}_{\text{l}} > \overline{V}_{\text{s}}\), hence the curves will shift to lower values when the pressure is reduced, as in Figure 12.2. Notice also that since \(\overline{V}_{\text{l}} \cong \overline{V}_{\text{s}}\), the shifts for both the solid and liquid lines are much smaller than the shift for the gas line. These shifts also translate to different values of the junctions, which means the phase changes will occur at different temperatures. Therefore both the melting point and the boiling point in general increase when pressure is increased (and vice versa). Notice how the change for the melting point is always much smaller than the change for the boiling point. Water is a noticeable exception to this trend because \(\overline{V}_{\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O,l}} < \overline{V}_{\text{ice}}\). This explains the experimental observation that increasing the pressure on ice causes the ice to melt.3
Considering the intersections between two lines, two phases are in equilibrium with each other at each of these points. For two or more phases to be in equilibrium, their chemical potentials must be equal:
\[
\mu_{\alpha} = \mu_{\beta}.
\tag{12.4}\]
If we now change either the temperature or the pressure, the location of the intersection will be shifted (see again Figure 12.2 and the discussion above). For infinitesimal changes in variables, the new location will be:
\[
\mu_{\alpha} + d\mu_{\alpha}= \mu_{\beta}+d\mu_{\beta},
\tag{12.5}\]
which using eq. 12.4, simply becomes:
\[
d\mu_{\alpha}= d\mu_{\beta}.
\tag{12.6}\]
Replacing the differential with the definition of chemical potential in eq. 12.1, we obtain:
\[
\begin{aligned}
-S_{\alpha}dT+\overline{V}_{\alpha}dP &= -S_{\beta}dT+\overline{V}_{\beta}dP \\
\underbrace{\left(S_{\beta}-S_{\alpha}\right)}_{\Delta S} dT &= \underbrace{\left( \overline{V}_{\beta}-\overline{V}_{\alpha}\right)}_{\Delta \overline{V}}dP,
\end{aligned}
\tag{12.7}\]
which can be rearranged into:
\[
\frac{dP}{dT}=\frac{\Delta S}{\Delta \overline{V}}.
\tag{12.8}\]
This equation is known as the Clapeyron equation, and it is the mathematical relation at the basis of the pressure-temperature phase diagrams. Plotting the results of eq. 12.8 on a \(PT\) phase diagram for common substances results in three lines representing the equilibrium between two different phases. These diagrams are useful to study the relationship between the phases of a substance.

title: 12  Phase Equilibrium
text:
12.2 Gibbs Phase Rule
In chapter 1, we have already seen that the number of independent variables required to describe an ideal gas is two. This number was derived by counting the total number of variables \((3: P,\overline{V},T)\), and reducing it by one because the ideal gas law constrains the value of one of them, once the other two are fixed. For a generic system potentially containing more than one chemical substance in several different phases, however, the number of independent variables can be different than two. For a system composed of \(c\) components (chemical substances) and \(p\) phases, the number of independent variables, \(f\), is given by the Gibbs phase rule:
\[
f=c-p+2.
\tag{12.9}\]
The Gibbs phase rule derives from the fact that different phases are in equilibrium with each other at some conditions, resulting in the reduction of the number of independent variables at those conditions. More rigorously, when two phases are in thermodynamic equilibrium, their chemical potentials are equal (see eq. 12.4). For each equality, the number of independent variables—also called the number of degrees of freedom—is reduced by one. For example, the chemical potentials of the liquid and its vapor depend on both \(T\) and \(P\). But when these phases are in equilibrium with each other, their chemical potentials must be equal. If either the pressure or the temperature is fixed, the other variable will be uniquely determined by the equality relation. In other terms, when a liquid is in equilibrium with its vapor at a given pressure, the temperature is determined by the fact that the chemical potentials of the two phases are the same, and is denoted as the boiling temperature \(T_{\text{b}}\). Similarly, at a given temperature, the pressure of the vapor is uniquely determined by the same equality relation and is denoted as the vapor pressure, \(P^*\).
The Gibbs phase rule is obtained considering that the number of independent variables is given by the total number of variables minus the constraints. The total number of variables is given by temperature, pressure, plus all the variables required to describe each of the phases. The composition of each phase is determined by \((c-1)\) variables.4 The number of constraints is determined by the number of possible equilibrium relations, which is \(c(p-1)\) since the chemical potential of each component must be equal in all phases. The number of degrees of freedom \(f\) is then given by \(f=(c-1)p+2-c(p-1)\) \(=c-p+2\), which is the Gibbs phase rule, as in eq. 12.9.

title: 12  Phase Equilibrium
text:
12.3 \(PT\) Phase Diagrams






Figure 12.3: The Pressure–Temperature Phase Diagram.



Let’s now discuss the pressure–temperature diagram of a typical substance, as reported in Figure 12.3. Each of the lines reported in the diagram represents an equilibrium between two phases, and therefore it represents a condition that reduces the number of degrees of freedom to one. The lines can be determined using the Clapeyron equation, eq. 12.8. The interpretation of each line is as follows:

12.3.1 Liquid \(\rightleftarrows\) Gas equilibrium
For this equilibrium we can use Trouton’s rule, eq. 7.7, and write: \[
\Delta_{\text{vap}} S = S_{\text{g}}-S_{\text{l}} \cong 88 \; \frac{\text{J}}{\text{mol K}} > 0\quad \text{always},
\tag{12.10}\]
where the entropy of vaporization is always positive, even for cases where the Trouton’s rule is violated. The difference in molar volumes is easily obtained, since the volume of the gas is always much greater than the volume of the liquid:
\[
\overline{V}_{\text{g}} - \overline{V}_{\text{l}} \cong \overline{V}_{\text{g}} = 22.4\; \frac{\text{L}}{\text{mol}} >0\quad \text{always}.
\tag{12.11}\]
Replacing these values in the Clapeyron equation, we obtain:
\[
\frac{dP}{dT}=\frac{88}{22.4}\left( \frac{0.0831}{8.31} \right) = 0.04\;\text{bar/K} > 0 \quad \text{always},
\tag{12.12}\]
which is always positive, regardless of violations to Trouton’s rule. Notice how small this value is, meaning that the liquid–gas equilibrium curve is mostly flat as \(T\rightarrow 0\).


12.3.2 Solid \(\rightleftarrows\) Gas equilibrium
If we look at the signs of each quantity, this case is similar to the previous one: \[
\begin{aligned}
\Delta_{\text{subl}} S &> 0 \quad \text{always} \\
\Delta_{\text{subl}} \overline{V }&> 0 \quad \text{always} \\
\\
\frac{dP}{dT} &> 0 \quad \text{always}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{12.13}\]
However, Trouton’s rule is not valid for the solid–gas equilibrium, and \(\frac{dP}{dT}\) will be larger than for the previous case.


12.3.3 Solid \(\rightleftarrows\) Liquid equilibrium
The final curve is for the solid-liquid equilibrium, for which we have:
\[
\Delta_{\text{fus}} S = \frac{\Delta_{\text{fus}} H}{T_{\text{m}}} > 0 \quad \text{always},
\tag{12.14}\]
since fusion is always an endothermic process, \((\Delta_{\text{fus}} H>0)\). On the other side:
\[
\Delta_{\text{fus}} \overline{V} = \overline{V}_{\text{l}} - \overline{V}_{\text{s}} > 0 \quad \text{generally}.
\]
In other words, the difference of the molar volume of the liquid and that of the solid is positive for most substances, but it might be negative (for example for \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\)). As such:
\[
\frac{dP}{dT} > 0 \quad \text{generally}.
\tag{12.15}\]
For \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\) and a few other substances, \(\frac{dP}{dT}<0\), an anomalous behavior that has crucial consequences for the existence of life on earth.5 Because of its importance, this behavior is also depicted in Figure 12.3 using a dashed green line.
Since the differences in molar volumes between the solid and the liquid phases are usually small (changes are generally of the order of \(10^{-3}\;\mathrm{L}\)), \(\frac{dP}{dT}\) is always much larger than for the previous two cases. The resulting lines for the solid–liquid equilibria are still almost vertical, regardless of the signs of their angular coefficients.


12.3.4 The triple point and the critical point
The only point in the \(PT\) diagram where all the three phases coexist is called the triple point. The number of degrees of freedom at the triple point for every 1-component diagram is \(f=1-3+2=0\). The fact that the triple point has zero degrees of freedom means that its coordinates, \(\{T_{\text{tp}},P_{\text{tp}},\overline{V}_{\text{tp}}\}\), are uniquely determined for each chemical substance. For this reason, the value of the triple point of water was fixed by definition—rather than measured—until 2019. This definition was necessary to establish the base unit of the thermodynamic temperature scale in the SI (the kelvin).6
In addition to the triple point where the solid, liquid, and gas phases meet, a triple point may involve more than one condensed phase. Triple points are common for substances with multiple solid phases (polymorphs), involving either two solid phases and a liquid one or three solid phases. Helium is a special case that presents a triple point involving two different fluid phases, called the lambda point. Since the number of degrees of freedom cannot be negative, the Gibbs phase rule for a 1-component diagram sets the limit to how many phases can coexist to just three. Therefore, quadruple points (or higher coexistence points) are not possible for pure substances, even for polymorphs.7
Another point with a fixed position in the \(PT\) diagram is the critical point, \(\{T_{\text{c}},P_{\text{c}},\overline{V}_{\text{c}}\}\). We have already given the definition of the critical temperature in definition 11.2. This point represents the end of the liquid–gas equilibrium curve. This point is also semantically important to define different regions of the phase diagram, as in Figure 12.3. A gas whose pressure and temperature are below the critical point is called a vapor. A gas whose temperature and pressure are above the critical ones is called a supercritical fluid. Finally, a liquid whose pressure is above the critical point is called a compressible liquid.8

text:
12.4 The Clausius–Clapeyron Equation
Let’s now take a closer look at the equilibrium between a condensed phase and the gas phase. For both the vaporization and sublimation processes, Clausius showed that the Clapeyron equation can be simplified by using:
\[
\Delta_{\text{vap}} S = \frac{\Delta_{\text{vap}} H}{T} \qquad \Delta \overline{V}= \overline{V}_{\mathrm{g}} -\overline{V}_{\mathrm{l}} \cong \overline{V}_{\mathrm{g}},
\tag{12.16}\]
resulting in:
\[
\frac{dP}{dT} = \frac{ \Delta_{\text{vap}} S}{\Delta \overline{V}} \cong \frac{ \Delta_{\text{vap}} H}{T \overline{V}_{\mathrm{g}}}.
\tag{12.17}\]
Using the ideal gas law to replace the molar volume of the gas, we obtain:
\[
\frac{dP}{dT} = \frac{P \Delta_{\text{vap}} H}{RT^2},
\tag{12.18}\]
which can be rearranged as:
\[
\frac{dP}{P} = \frac{\Delta_{\text{vap}} H}{R} \frac{dT}{T^2}.
\tag{12.19}\]
Eq. 12.19 is known as the Clausius–Clapeyron equation, and it measures the dependence of the vapor pressure of a substance as a function of the temperature. The Clausius–Clapeyron equation can be integrated to obtain:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\int_{P_i}^{P_f} \frac{dP}{P} &= \frac{\Delta_{\text{vap}} H}{R} \int_{T_i}^{T_f} \frac{dT}{T^2} \\
\ln \frac{P_f}{P_i} &=-\frac{\Delta_{\text{vap}} H}{R} \left( \frac{1}{T_f}-\frac{1}{T_i} \right).
\end{aligned}
\tag{12.20}\]
The integrated Clausius–Clapeyron equation shows that the vapor pressure depends exponentially on the temperature. Thus, even a small change in the temperature will result in a significant change in the vapor pressure. In fact, we daily use the fact that the vapor pressure of water changes drastically when we increase its temperature for cooking most of our food. For example, at an external pressure of 1 bar, it rapidly grows from \(P^*=0.02\;\text{bar}\) to \(P^*=1\;\text{bar}\) when the temperature is increased from \(T=293\;\mathrm{K}\) (around room temperature) to \(T=373\;\mathrm{K}\) (boiling point). The integrated Clausius–Clapeyron equation is also often used to determine the enthalpy of vaporization from measurements of vapor pressure at different temperatures.

text:
12.5 Chapter Review

12.5.1 Study Questions
1. What is the definition of a phase in thermodynamics?

A region of the system with heterogeneous chemical composition.
A region of the system with homogeneous chemical composition and physical state.
A region of the system with constant temperature and pressure.
A region of the system with varying density and volume.
A region of the system with uniform crystal structure.


2. According to the Gibbs phase rule, how many degrees of freedom (\(f\)) does a system with 2 components (\(c\)) and 3 phases (\(p\)) have?

\(f = 1\).
\(f = 2\).
\(f = 3\).
\(f = 4\).
\(f = 5\).


3. Which of the following statements about the triple point is correct?

It has one degree of freedom for a one-component system.
It represents the coexistence of four phases.
Its coordinates are uniquely determined for each chemical substance.
It always occurs at standard temperature and pressure.
It is the point where all phases become identical.


4. What does the Clausius-Clapeyron equation describe?

The dependence of critical temperature on pressure.
The relationship between enthalpy and entropy of vaporization.
The dependence of vapor pressure on temperature.
The relationship between molar volume and critical pressure.
The dependence of boiling point on atmospheric pressure.


5. Which of the following is true about the entropy change during vaporization?

It is always negative.
It is approximately equal to \(88\,\text{J/(mol·K)}\) for many substances (Trouton’s rule).
It decreases with increasing temperature.
It is always zero at the critical point.
It is the same for all substances at their normal boiling points.


6. What is the typical shape of the solid-liquid equilibrium line in a P-T phase diagram for most substances?

Nearly horizontal.
Nearly vertical with a positive slope.
Nearly vertical with a negative slope.
Parabolic.
Exponential.


7. Which of the following is true about the critical point?

It represents the end of the solid-liquid equilibrium curve.
It is the point where all three phases (solid, liquid, gas) coexist.
Its pressure is always \(1\,\text{atm}\).
It represents the end of the liquid-gas equilibrium curve.
It is the point where the substance changes directly from solid to gas.


8. What is the mathematical expression for the Clapeyron equation?

\(\frac{dP}{dT} = \frac{\Delta S}{\Delta V}\).
\(\frac{dP}{dT} = \frac{\Delta H}{T\Delta V}\).
\(\frac{dP}{dT} = \frac{\Delta G}{\Delta V}\).
\(\frac{dP}{dT} = \frac{\Delta H}{\Delta S}\).
\(\frac{dP}{dT} = \frac{T\Delta S}{\Delta V}\).


9. Which of the following is an anomalous behavior exhibited by water?

Its solid phase is less dense than its liquid phase.
Its boiling point increases with increasing pressure.
Its triple point is at \(0\,\text{°C}\) and \(1\,\text{atm}\).
Its critical point is at \(100\,\text{°C}\).
Its solid-liquid equilibrium line has a positive slope in the P-T diagram.


10. What is the definition of a supercritical fluid?

A fluid at a temperature below its critical point and pressure above its critical point.
A fluid at a temperature and pressure both above its critical point.
A fluid at a temperature above its critical point and pressure below its critical point.
A fluid at its triple point.
A fluid at standard temperature and pressure.








TipAnswers





1.b, 2.a, 3.c, 4.c, 5.b, 6.b, 7.d, 8.a, 9.a, 10.b

title: 12  Phase Equilibrium
text:
Other states of matter—such as plasma—are possible, but they are not usually observed at the values of temperature and pressure that classical thermodynamics is usually applied to. Discussion of these extreme cases is beyond the scope of this textbook.↩︎
Think, for example, of the integral \(\int SdT\), for which we can assume \(S\) independent of temperature to obtain \(S\Delta T\). In practice, the entropy increases slightly with the temperature. Therefore the curves in Figure 12.1 are slightly concave downwards (remember that they are obtained from values of \(-S\), so if \(S\) increases with \(T\), the curves bend downwards.)↩︎
Despite the effect being minimal, it is one of the contributing causes to the fact that we can skate on ice, but we can’t on stone. If we increase our pressure on ice by reducing our footprints’ surface area using thin skates, ice will slightly melt under our own weight, creating a thin liquid film on which we can skate because of the reduced friction.↩︎
For a 1-component system \(c-1=1-1=0\), and no additional variable is required to determine the composition of each phase. For a 2-component system, however, each phase will contain both components, hence \(c-1=2-1=1\) additional variable will be required to describe it–the mole fraction.↩︎
As is well explained by Wikipedia’s article on the properties of water: “The unusual density curve and lower density of ice than of water is vital to life—if water were most dense at the freezing point, then in winter the very cold water at the surface of lakes and other water bodies would sink, lakes could freeze from the bottom up, and all life in them would be killed. Furthermore, given that water is a good thermal insulator (due to its heat capacity), some frozen lakes might not completely thaw in summer. The layer of ice that floats on top insulates the water below. Water at about 4 °C (39 °F) also sinks to the bottom, thus keeping the temperature of the water at the bottom constant.”↩︎
For more information on the 2019 redefinition of the SI units, see Wikipedia’s article on the 2019 redefinition of the SI base units.↩︎
Notice that quadruple points are possible for 2-component diagrams.↩︎
Notice that the temperature of a liquid must be below the critical point, otherwise it is no longer a liquid but rather a supercritical fluid.↩︎

title: 13  Multi-Component Phase Diagrams and Solutions
text:
13.1 Describing a Two-Component System
In chapter 12, we studied what happens when a single substance is split between two or more phases, and we used the chemical potential to understand when, for example, a liquid boils or a solid melts. Most of the chemistry we do in the lab, however, does not involve pure substances, but mixtures: we dissolve salts in water, we mix solvents, we bubble gases through liquids. In this chapter, we will extend the ideas of the previous chapter to systems that contain two or more chemical species. As we will see, the presence of a second component opens up a whole new set of phenomena that are extremely useful in practice, from the separation of liquids by distillation to the reason why we spread salt on icy roads in winter.
Systems that include two or more chemical species in the same phase are usually called solutions. The species present in the largest amount is usually called the solvent, and the others are called solutes. Solutions are possible for all three states of matter:
Let’s start by counting how many variables we need to describe a solution of two components (a binary solution). Recalling the Gibbs phase rule from chapter 12, the number of degrees of freedom for \(c=2\) components is:
\[
f=2-p+2=4-p.
\tag{13.1}\]
A few important considerations can be made by analyzing eq. 13.1:

13  Multi-Component Phase Diagrams and Solutions

title: 13  Multi-Component Phase Diagrams and Solutions
text:
One phase needs three variables. When the solution is in a single phase (e.g., a liquid), we need \(4-1=3\) variables to describe it. These are usually the temperature, \(T\), the pressure, \(P\), and the composition. For two components, the composition is given by a single mole fraction, since the other one is obtained from \(x_{\text{A}}+x_{\text{B}}=1\). We will use \(x_i\) for the mole fractions in the liquid phase and \(y_i\) for those in the gas phase.
Three variables would require a 3D plot. To represent all states of a single-phase binary system, we would need a three-dimensional \(T,P,x\) diagram. Since 3D plots are hard to draw and to read, we will always keep one of the variables constant: either the temperature (obtaining a \(Px\) diagram) or the pressure (obtaining a \(Tx\) diagram).
Two phases leave two variables. When a liquid and its vapor coexist, \(f=4-2=2\). If we also fix the temperature, only one variable remains free. In other words, at a given temperature, once we choose the composition of the liquid, the pressure and the composition of the vapor are fixed by nature. This is what makes the diagrams in this chapter so useful: they tell us exactly what vapor will form above a given liquid.

title: 13  Multi-Component Phase Diagrams and Solutions
text:
13.2 Ideal Solutions and Raoult’s Law
In chapter 11, we simplified the treatment of gases by introducing the ideal gas, a model where molecules do not interact with each other. For liquids, this assumption is simply impossible, since the interactions between molecules are what keeps a liquid together in the first place. We need, therefore, a different kind of simplification:

Definition 13.1 Ideal solution: A solution where the interactions between molecules of different species (\(\mathrm{A}\)–\(\mathrm{B}\)) are, on average, the same as the interactions between molecules of the same species (\(\mathrm{A}\)–\(\mathrm{A}\) and \(\mathrm{B}\)–\(\mathrm{B}\)).

In an ideal solution, a molecule of \(\mathrm{A}\) does not “notice” whether its neighbors are molecules of \(\mathrm{A}\) or \(\mathrm{B}\). This has two immediate consequences: mixing the two liquids releases or absorbs no heat (\(\Delta_{\text{mix}}H=0\)), and the volume of the mixture is the sum of the volumes of the two liquids (\(\Delta_{\text{mix}}V=0\)). The only thing that changes upon mixing is the number of ways in which we can arrange the molecules, which increases. As we saw in chapter 6, this means that the entropy increases, and that mixing in an ideal solution is a spontaneous process driven entirely by entropy. Mixtures of chemically similar molecules, such as benzene and toluene, or hexane and heptane, behave as ideal solutions to a very good approximation. We will also assume that the vapor above the solution behaves as a mixture of ideal gases, which is reasonable at the low pressures that we usually deal with.
What is the vapor pressure of an ideal solution? Let’s think about a molecule of \(\mathrm{A}\) at the surface of the liquid. Its tendency to escape into the gas phase depends on how strongly it is held by its neighbors. In an ideal solution, the neighbors hold it exactly as strongly as in the pure liquid, so each molecule of \(\mathrm{A}\) at the surface escapes as easily as it would from pure \(\mathrm{A}\). However, only a fraction \(x_{\text{A}}\) of the molecules at the surface are molecules of \(\mathrm{A}\). It is then reasonable to expect that the partial pressure of \(\mathrm{A}\) above the solution is the vapor pressure of pure \(\mathrm{A}\), reduced by this fraction. This plausibility argument is confirmed experimentally, and it was formulated by François-Marie Raoult (1830–1901) in what is known as Raoult’s law:
\[
P_i=x_i P_i^*,
\tag{13.2}\]
where \(P_i\) is the partial pressure of component \(i\) above the solution, \(x_i\) is its mole fraction in the liquid, and \(P_i^*\) is the vapor pressure of pure \(i\) at the same temperature. Raoult’s law can also be used as an alternative definition of an ideal solution: a solution is ideal if all of its components follow eq. 13.2 at all compositions.

13.2.1 One volatile component
Let’s first consider a solution where only one of the two components, \(\mathrm{A}\), is volatile. This is the case, for example, of a solution of sugar in water, since sugar has no measurable vapor pressure. In this case, the pressure above the solution is entirely due to \(\mathrm{A}\), and Raoult’s law describes a straight line in the \(Px_{\text{B}}\) diagram, going from \(P_{\text{A}}^*\) for pure \(\mathrm{A}\) (\(x_{\text{B}}=0\)) to zero for pure \(\mathrm{B}\) (\(x_{\text{B}}=1\)), as in Figure 13.1.






Figure 13.1: The Pressure–Composition Phase Diagram of an Ideal Solution Containing a Single Volatile Component at Constant Temperature.



A few important considerations can be made by analyzing Figure 13.1:

The line separates two regions. Above the line, the pressure is higher than the vapor pressure of the solution, and only the liquid is stable. Below the line, the pressure is lower, the liquid evaporates, and only the vapor is stable. Each region has \(f=3\) degrees of freedom, but only two of them are visible in the diagram, since the temperature is kept constant.
Along the line, liquid and vapor coexist. Raoult’s law acts as an additional constraint for the points on the line, which have only two degrees of freedom. Since the temperature is fixed, choosing the composition of the liquid determines the pressure, and vice versa.
Adding a nonvolatile solute lowers the vapor pressure. Moving from left to right along the line, the vapor pressure decreases. This is the first example of a colligative property, which we will discuss in detail at the end of this chapter.



13.2.2 Two volatile components
When both components are volatile, each of them follows Raoult’s law, and both contribute to the vapor. Since we are treating the vapor as a mixture of ideal gases, the total pressure is simply the sum of the two partial pressures, according to Dalton’s law, eq. 9.23:
\[
P_{\text{TOT}}=P_{\text{A}}+P_{\text{B}}=x_{\text{A}}P_{\text{A}}^*+x_{\text{B}}P_{\text{B}}^*=P_{\text{A}}^*+x_{\text{B}}\left(P_{\text{B}}^*-P_{\text{A}}^*\right),
\tag{13.3}\]
where in the last step we used \(x_{\text{A}}=1-x_{\text{B}}\). Eq. 13.3 is the equation of a straight line that goes from \(P_{\text{A}}^*\) to \(P_{\text{B}}^*\), as reported in red in Figure 13.2. The partial pressures of each of the two components are also reported, using black dotted lines.






Figure 13.2: The Pressure–Composition Phase Diagram of an Ideal Solution Containing Two Volatile Components at Constant Temperature.




Exercise 13.1 Calculate the mole fraction in the vapor phase of a liquid solution composed of 67% of toluene (\(\mathrm{A}\)) and 33% of benzene (\(\mathrm{B}\)) (in moles), given the vapor pressures of the pure substances: \(P_{\text{A}}^*=0.03\;\text{bar}\), and \(P_{\text{B}}^*=0.10\;\text{bar}\).
Solution: The data available for the system are summarized as follows: \[
\begin{aligned}
x_{\text{A}}=0.67  \qquad & \qquad x_{\text{B}}=0.33 \\
P_{\text{A}}^* = 0.03\;\text{bar} \qquad & \qquad P_{\text{B}}^* = 0.10\;\text{bar} \\
& P_{\text{TOT}} = ? \\
y_{\text{A}}=? \qquad & \qquad y_{\text{B}}=?
\end{aligned}
\tag{13.4}\] The partial pressures and the total pressure of the vapors can be calculated combining Raoult’s and Dalton’s laws: \[
\begin{aligned}
P_{\text{A}} &= x_{\text{A}} P_{\text{A}}^* = 0.67\cdot 0.03 = 0.020\;\text{bar} \\
P_{\text{B}} &= x_{\text{B}} P_{\text{B}}^* = 0.33\cdot 0.10 = 0.033\;\text{bar} \\
P_{\text{TOT}} &= P_{\text{A}}+P_{\text{B}} = 0.053 \;\text{bar}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{13.5}\] Since each partial pressure is proportional to the number of moles of that component in the vapor, we can calculate the mole fractions in the vapor phase as: \[
\begin{aligned}
y_{\text{A}}=\frac{P_{\text{A}}}{P_{\text{TOT}}} & \qquad y_{\text{B}}=\frac{P_{\text{B}}}{P_{\text{TOT}}} \\
y_{\text{A}}=\frac{0.020}{0.053}=0.38 & \qquad y_{\text{B}}=\frac{0.033}{0.053}=0.62.
\end{aligned}
\tag{13.6}\] Notice how the vapor is much richer in benzene (\(y_{\text{B}}=0.62\)) than the liquid (\(x_{\text{B}}=0.33\)). Benzene has the higher vapor pressure (it is more volatile), so its molecules escape more easily into the gas phase.

The result of Exercise 13.1 is completely general: the vapor above an ideal solution is always richer in the more volatile component than the liquid it comes from. Since the compositions of the liquid and of the vapor are different, we can report both of them in the same diagram, as in Figure 13.3. The line that gives the composition of the liquid, \(x_{\text{B}}\), is called the liquidus line (or bubble point line), while the line that gives the composition of the vapor, \(y_{\text{B}}\), is called the dew point line.






Figure 13.3: The Pressure–Composition Phase Diagram of an Ideal Solution Containing Two Volatile Components at Constant Temperature. Both the Liquidus and Dew Point Line are Emphasized in this Plot.



The liquidus and dew point lines enclose a new region of the diagram, where the liquid and the vapor coexist. Let’s follow the arrow in Figure 13.3 to understand how to read this diagram:

We start from a liquid with composition \(x^i_{\text{B}}\) at high pressure (point \(i\)). Here only the liquid is stable.
We lower the pressure at constant temperature and composition, moving straight down, until we hit the liquidus line. At this pressure, the liquid starts to boil.
The first bubble of vapor that forms does not have the same composition as the liquid. Its composition is found by moving horizontally (at the same pressure) until we hit the dew point line, which gives \(y^f_{\text{B}}\). As expected, the vapor is richer in the more volatile component, \(\mathrm{B}\).
Inside the coexistence region, any horizontal line (called a tie line) connects a liquid and a vapor in equilibrium with each other. Since there are only two degrees of freedom inside this region, and the temperature is fixed, once we fix the pressure, the compositions of both phases are determined.



13.2.3 \(Tx_{\text{B}}\) phase diagrams and fractional distillation
In the lab, we usually boil liquids at constant (atmospheric) pressure by increasing the temperature, rather than by reducing the pressure. It is therefore more useful to look at the phase diagram of a 2-component ideal solution as a function of temperature at constant pressure. The \(Tx_{\text{B}}\) diagram for two volatile components is reported in Figure 13.4. Notice that, in this diagram, the more volatile component is \(\mathrm{A}\), which has the lower boiling point, \(T_{\text{b}}^{\text{A}}\).






Figure 13.4: The Temperature–Composition Phase Diagram of an Ideal Solution Containing Two Volatile Components at Constant Pressure.



A few important considerations can be made by analyzing Figure 13.4:

The phases are in reversed order. Compared to the \(Px_{\text{B}}\) diagram of Figure 13.3, the liquid is now at the bottom (low temperature), and the vapor is on top (high temperature).
The two lines form a lens. The liquidus and dew point lines are curved, and they enclose a lens-shaped region where liquid and vapor coexist. Inside the lens there are only two degrees of freedom, and since the pressure is kept constant, only one of them is visible in the plot: if we choose the temperature, the compositions of both phases are fixed, and vice versa.
A mixture boils over a range of temperatures. If we heat a liquid of composition \(x_{\text{B}}^i\), it starts boiling when it hits the liquidus line. The first vapor that forms has composition \(y_{\text{B}}^f\), which is richer in the more volatile component \(\mathrm{A}\). As the vapor leaves, the remaining liquid becomes richer in \(\mathrm{B}\), and its boiling temperature increases. Unlike a pure substance, a mixture does not have a single boiling point.

The difference in composition between the liquid and the vapor can be exploited to separate the two components. If we collect the vapor and condense it, we obtain a liquid that is richer in \(\mathrm{A}\) than the one we started from. If we boil this new liquid again, its vapor will be even richer in \(\mathrm{A}\). Each evaporation and condensation step corresponds to a horizontal line (from the liquidus line to the dew point line) followed by a vertical line (from the dew point line down to the liquidus line), as in the staircase of Figure 13.5. Each of these steps is called a theoretical plate, and by repeating it enough times we can obtain almost pure \(\mathrm{A}\). This is the principle of fractional distillation.






Figure 13.5: The Fractional Distillation Process and Theoretical Plates Calculated on a Temperature–Composition Phase Diagram.



In practice, the evaporations and condensations do not happen in separate flasks, but along a tall column filled with trays, as schematically depicted on the right of Figure 13.5. The mixture is heated at the bottom, and the temperature decreases with the height of the column. On each tray, the rising vapor partially condenses and the liquid partially evaporates, so that each tray works as one theoretical plate. The vapor collected at the top is rich in the most volatile component, while the liquid collected at the bottom is rich in the least volatile one. Counting the theoretical plates on the \(Tx_{\text{B}}\) diagram tells chemical engineers how many trays a column needs to reach the desired purity, which is how industrial distillation columns are sized.

title: 13  Multi-Component Phase Diagrams and Solutions
text:
13.3 Phase Diagrams of Non-Ideal Solutions
In most real solutions, the \(\mathrm{A}\)–\(\mathrm{B}\) interactions are not the same as the \(\mathrm{A}\)–\(\mathrm{A}\) and \(\mathrm{B}\)–\(\mathrm{B}\) ones, and Raoult’s law is followed only over a small range of compositions. Let’s start again from a solution with a single volatile component, \(\mathrm{A}\), whose typical behavior is reported in the \(Px_{\text{B}}\) plot of Figure 13.6.






Figure 13.6: The Pressure–Composition Phase Diagram of a Non-Ideal Solution Containing a Single Volatile Component at Constant Temperature.



A few important considerations can be made by analyzing Figure 13.6:

When \(\mathrm{A}\) is abundant (\(x_{\text{B}} \rightarrow 0\)), Raoult’s law holds. In this region, \(\mathrm{A}\) is the solvent, and almost every molecule of \(\mathrm{A}\) is surrounded by other molecules of \(\mathrm{A}\), as in the pure liquid. Its escaping tendency is therefore the same as in pure \(\mathrm{A}\), as Raoult’s law assumes.
When \(\mathrm{A}\) is dilute (\(x_{\text{B}} \rightarrow 1\)), Henry’s law holds. In this region, \(\mathrm{A}\) is the solute, and each molecule of \(\mathrm{A}\) is surrounded almost exclusively by molecules of \(\mathrm{B}\). Its escaping tendency is now determined by the \(\mathrm{A}\)–\(\mathrm{B}\) interactions, which are different from the \(\mathrm{A}\)–\(\mathrm{A}\) ones. The partial pressure is still proportional to the mole fraction, but with a different proportionality constant, as shown by the green dotted line.
In between, neither law holds, and the curve must be measured experimentally.

The law that describes the dilute region was found by William Henry (1774–1836), who extensively studied the behavior of gases dissolved in liquids. Henry’s law states that the partial pressure of a dilute solute \(i\) is proportional to its mole fraction in the solution:
\[
P_i=k_{\text{H},i}\, x_i \qquad \text{(for } x_i \rightarrow 0\text{)},
\tag{13.7}\]
where the Henry’s law constant, \(k_{\text{H},i}\), depends on the chemical nature of both the solute and the solvent, and on the temperature. Henry’s law is commonly used for gases dissolved in liquids. For example, the amount of \(\mathrm{CO}_2\) dissolved in a carbonated drink is proportional to the pressure of \(\mathrm{CO}_2\) above it, which is why the drink goes flat when we open the bottle and the pressure drops. In a dilute solution, the solvent follows Raoult’s law, while the solute follows Henry’s law.
When both components are volatile, the total pressure is once again the sum of the two partial pressures. Two different behaviors are possible, depending on the strength of the \(\mathrm{A}\)–\(\mathrm{B}\) interactions, as reported in Figure 13.7:

Positive deviation (left panel): the \(\mathrm{A}\)–\(\mathrm{B}\) interactions are weaker than the \(\mathrm{A}\)–\(\mathrm{A}\) and \(\mathrm{B}\)–\(\mathrm{B}\) ones. The molecules are held less strongly in the mixture than in the pure liquids, they escape more easily, and the vapor pressure is higher than the one predicted by Raoult’s law. Mixing these liquids typically absorbs heat (\(\Delta_{\text{mix}}H>0\)). An example is the acetone/carbon disulfide mixture.
Negative deviation (right panel): the \(\mathrm{A}\)–\(\mathrm{B}\) interactions are stronger than the \(\mathrm{A}\)–\(\mathrm{A}\) and \(\mathrm{B}\)–\(\mathrm{B}\) ones (for example, because \(\mathrm{A}\) and \(\mathrm{B}\) form hydrogen bonds with each other). The molecules are held more strongly, and the vapor pressure is lower than the one predicted by Raoult’s law. Mixing these liquids typically releases heat (\(\Delta_{\text{mix}}H<0\)). Examples are the acetone/chloroform and the hydrochloric acid/water mixtures. Negative deviations are slightly less common than positive ones.







Figure 13.7: The Pressure–Composition Phase Diagram of Non-Ideal Solutions Containing Two Volatile Components at Constant Temperature.



If we move from the \(Px_{\text{B}}\) diagram to the \(Tx_{\text{B}}\) diagram, the behaviors observed in Figure 13.7 correspond to the diagrams in Figure 13.8. Since a higher vapor pressure means that the mixture boils at a lower temperature, a maximum in the \(Px_{\text{B}}\) diagram becomes a minimum in the \(Tx_{\text{B}}\) diagram, and vice versa.






Figure 13.8: The Temperature–Composition Phase Diagram of Non-Ideal Solutions Containing Two Volatile Components at Constant Pressure.



The minimum (left plot) and maximum (right plot) points in Figure 13.8 are called azeotropes. At an azeotrope, the liquidus and dew point lines touch, so the liquid and the vapor have the same composition. If we boil a mixture with the azeotropic composition, the vapor has the same composition as the liquid, and distillation cannot change it. The mixture boils at a single temperature, as if it was a pure substance. In practice, distillation can bring us to the azeotrope, but not past it. Two types of azeotropes exist, corresponding to the two types of deviation:

Positive (minimum-boiling) azeotrope (left plot in Figure 13.8). A well-known example is the ethanol/water mixture at atmospheric pressure, with composition 95.6% ethanol by mass. This azeotrope boils at \(T=78.2\;^\circ \text{C}\), a temperature that is lower than the boiling points of both pure constituents (ethanol boils at \(T=78.4\;^\circ \text{C}\) and water at \(T=100\;^\circ \text{C}\)). This is why we cannot obtain pure ethanol from fermented mixtures by simple distillation.
Negative (maximum-boiling) azeotrope (right plot in Figure 13.8). An example is the hydrochloric acid/water mixture at atmospheric pressure, with composition 20.2% hydrochloric acid by mass. This azeotrope boils at about \(T=110\;^\circ \text{C}\), a temperature that is higher than the boiling points of both pure constituents (hydrochloric acid boils at \(T=-84\;^\circ \text{C}\) and water at \(T=100\;^\circ \text{C}\)).

title: 13  Multi-Component Phase Diagrams and Solutions
text:
13.4 Activity
To treat non-ideal solutions quantitatively, we need a quantity that plays the same role that the mole fraction plays in Raoult’s law. We did something very similar for non-ideal gases in chapter 11, where we replaced the pressure with the fugacity, an effective pressure. For solutions, we will replace the mole fraction with an effective mole fraction, called the activity. Let’s derive it step by step, using the vapor above the solution as a “probe” of what happens in the liquid.

The vapor. Assuming that the vapor behaves as an ideal gas, the chemical potential of component \(i\) in the vapor is given by eq. 11.28: \[
\mu_i^{\text{vapor}} = \mu_i^{\standardstate} + RT \ln \frac{P_i}{P^{\standardstate}}.
\tag{13.8}\]
Equilibrium with the solution. If the vapor is in equilibrium with the solution, the chemical potential of \(i\) must be the same in both phases (eq. 12.4): \[
\mu_i^{\text{solution}} = \mu_i^{\text{vapor}} = \mu_i^{\standardstate} + RT \ln \frac{P_i}{P^{\standardstate}}.
\tag{13.9}\]
The pure liquid as a reference. The same reasoning applies to the pure liquid \(i\), which is in equilibrium with its vapor at the pressure \(P_i^*\). Its chemical potential, \(\mu_i^*\), is therefore: \[
\mu_i^* = \mu_i^{\standardstate} + RT \ln \frac{P_i^*}{P^{\standardstate}}.
\tag{13.10}\]
Subtracting eq. 13.10 from eq. 13.9, the standard chemical potential of the gas and the standard pressure cancel out, and we obtain: \[
\mu_i^{\text{solution}} = \mu_i^* + RT \ln \frac{P_i}{P^*_i}.
\tag{13.11}\]

Eq. 13.11 tells us that the ratio \(P_i/P_i^*\) measures how much the chemical potential of \(i\) in the solution differs from that of the pure liquid. We call this ratio the activity of component \(i\):
\[
a_i = \frac{P_i}{P_i^*} \qquad \Rightarrow \qquad \mu_i^{\text{solution}} = \mu_i^* + RT \ln a_i.
\tag{13.12}\]
A few important considerations can be made by analyzing eq. 13.12:

For an ideal solution, the activity is the mole fraction. Using Raoult’s law, eq. 13.2, \(a_i=x_i\), and eq. 13.12 becomes: \[
\mu_i^{\text{solution}} = \mu_i^* + RT \ln x_i.
\tag{13.13}\] Since \(x_i<1\), the logarithm is negative, and the chemical potential of a component in an ideal solution is always lower than that of the pure liquid. This is the same result we found for mixtures of ideal gases in chapter 9, and it is the reason why ideal solutions form spontaneously.
For a non-ideal solution, the activity is an effective mole fraction. We can write it as the mole fraction multiplied by a correction factor, called the activity coefficient, \(\gamma_i\): \[
a_i = \gamma_i x_i \qquad \Rightarrow \qquad \mu_i^{\text{solution}} = \mu_i^* + RT \ln \left(\gamma_i x_i\right).
\tag{13.14}\]
The activity coefficient is measured from the vapor pressure. Combining eq. 13.12 and eq. 13.14: \[
\gamma_i = \frac{P_i}{x_i P_i^*} = \frac{P_i}{P_i^{\text{R}}},
\tag{13.15}\] where \(P_i^{\text{R}}=x_i P_i^*\) is the partial pressure predicted by Raoult’s law. For a positive deviation, the measured pressure is higher than the Raoult one, and \(\gamma_i>1\). For a negative deviation, it is lower, and \(0<\gamma_i<1\). For an ideal solution, \(\gamma_i=1\). This procedure is illustrated in Figure 13.9.
The activity is a relative quantity. It measures the “escaping tendency” of a component relative to a reference state, which in this case is the pure liquid at the same temperature and pressure, for which \(a_i=1\). This choice of reference (standard state) is a convention. We could choose a different one, and the values of the activities would change accordingly, but the physics would not. For gases, the standard state is the ideal gas at \(P^{\standardstate}=1\;\text{bar}\), and the activity is \(f/P^{\standardstate}\).







Figure 13.9: Positive and Negative Deviation from Raoult’s Law in the Pressure–Composition Phase Diagram of Non-Ideal Solutions at Constant Temperature.



As we already discussed in chapter 10, the activity is the most general quantity that we can use to define the equilibrium constant of a reaction (or the reaction quotient). The advantage of using the activity is that it’s defined for ideal and non-ideal gases and mixtures of gases, as well as for ideal and non-ideal solutions in both the liquid and the solid phase.1

title: 13  Multi-Component Phase Diagrams and Solutions
text:
13.5 Colligative Properties
Colligative properties are properties of solutions that depend on the number of solute particles in the solution, and not on their chemical nature. They usually appear when we dissolve a nonvolatile solute (such as sugar or salt) in a volatile liquid solvent (such as water), and they are properties of the solvent, modified by the presence of the solute. We will discuss four of them: the lowering of the vapor pressure, the elevation of the boiling point, the depression of the melting point, and the osmotic pressure.
All four of them have the same origin, which we have already found in eq. 13.13. In an ideal solution, the chemical potential of the solvent is:
\[
\mu_{\text{solvent}}^{\text{solution}} = \mu_{\text{solvent}}^* + RT \ln x_{\text{solvent}} < \mu_{\text{solvent}}^*.
\tag{13.16}\]
In other words, dissolving a solute always lowers the chemical potential of the solvent. This lowering is not due to any special interaction between solute and solvent. In an ideal solution there is none: it is a purely entropic effect, due to the increased number of ways in which the molecules can be arranged in the mixture. This is also why the result depends only on the mole fraction, and not on what the solute is. At the same time, the phases that contain only pure solvent (the vapor above the solution, since the solute is nonvolatile, and the solid, since the solute usually does not dissolve in the solid solvent) are not affected at all. The liquid is therefore stabilized with respect to both the vapor and the solid, as shown in Figure 13.10. For non-ideal solutions, the formulas that we will derive below are only valid approximately, but they work well for dilute solutions.






Figure 13.10: Reduction of the Chemical Potential of the Liquid Phase Due to the Addition of a Solute.



For dilute solutions, the most useful measure of concentration is the molality, \(m\), defined as the number of moles of solute divided by the mass of the solvent in kilograms:2
\[
m = \frac{n_{\text{solute}}}{m_{\text{solvent}}}.
\tag{13.17}\]
For a dilute solution, the mole fraction of the solute is related to the molality by a simple approximation. Since \(n_{\text{solute}} \ll n_{\text{solvent}}\):
\[
x_{\text{solute}}=\frac{n_{\text{solute}}}{n_{\text{solute}}+n_{\text{solvent}}} \approx \frac{n_{\text{solute}}}{n_{\text{solvent}}} = \frac{n_{\text{solute}}}{m_{\text{solvent}}/M} = mM,
\tag{13.18}\]
where \(M\) is the molar mass of the solvent, in \(\text{kg/mol}\).

13.5.1 Vapor pressure lowering
As we have already seen in Figure 13.1, the vapor pressure above a solution of a nonvolatile solute follows Raoult’s law. Its difference with respect to the vapor pressure of the pure solvent is:
\[
\begin{aligned}
P_{\text{solvent}}^* &- P_{\text{solution}} = P_{\text{solvent}}^* - x_{\text{solvent}} P_{\text{solvent}}^* \\
& = \left( 1-x_{\text{solvent}}\right)P_{\text{solvent}}^* =x_{\text{solute}} P_{\text{solvent}}^*,
\end{aligned}
\tag{13.19}\]
which shows that the vapor pressure lowering depends only on the mole fraction of the solute, and not on its nature. As such, it is a colligative property.


13.5.2 Boiling point elevation and melting point depression
Let’s now look at Figure 13.10 again. Since the chemical potential of the liquid is lowered, its line crosses the line of the gas at a higher temperature, and the line of the solid at a lower temperature. Therefore, the boiling point increases, and the melting point decreases. To find out by how much, let’s follow the boiling point step by step.3

The equilibrium condition. At the boiling point of the solution, \(T_{\text{b}}\), the chemical potential of the pure vapor equals that of the solvent in the solution, eq. 13.16: \[
\mu_{\text{gas}}^*(T_{\text{b}}) = \mu_{\text{liquid}}^*(T_{\text{b}}) + RT_{\text{b}}\ln x_{\text{solvent}} \quad \Rightarrow \quad \ln x_{\text{solvent}} = \frac{\mu_{\text{gas}}^*-\mu_{\text{liquid}}^*}{RT_{\text{b}}}=\frac{\Delta_{\text{vap}}G(T_{\text{b}})}{RT_{\text{b}}},
\tag{13.20}\] where \(\Delta_{\text{vap}}G\) is the molar Gibbs energy of vaporization of the pure solvent.
The Gibbs–Helmholtz equation. We know that \(\Delta_{\text{vap}}G=0\) at the boiling point of the pure solvent, \(T_{\text{b}}^*\). We can find its value at \(T_{\text{b}}\) by integrating the Gibbs–Helmholtz equation, eq. 9.9, between \(T_{\text{b}}^*\) and \(T_{\text{b}}\), assuming that \(\Delta_{\text{vap}}H\) is constant: \[
\frac{\Delta_{\text{vap}}G(T_{\text{b}})}{T_{\text{b}}} = \Delta_{\text{vap}}H \left(\frac{1}{T_{\text{b}}}-\frac{1}{T_{\text{b}}^*}\right) \quad \Rightarrow \quad \ln x_{\text{solvent}} = \frac{\Delta_{\text{vap}}H}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T_{\text{b}}}-\frac{1}{T_{\text{b}}^*}\right).
\tag{13.21}\]
The dilute-solution approximations. For a dilute solution, \(\ln x_{\text{solvent}}=\ln (1-x_{\text{solute}}) \approx -x_{\text{solute}}\), and since \(T_{\text{b}}\) and \(T_{\text{b}}^*\) are very close to each other, \(\frac{1}{T_{\text{b}}}-\frac{1}{T_{\text{b}}^*}=\frac{T_{\text{b}}^*-T_{\text{b}}}{T_{\text{b}}T_{\text{b}}^*} \approx -\frac{\Delta T_{\text{b}}}{\left(T_{\text{b}}^*\right)^2}\). Replacing both into eq. 13.21, and using eq. 13.18 for the mole fraction of the solute: \[
\Delta T_{\text{b}} = \frac{R\left(T_{\text{b}}^*\right)^2}{\Delta_{\text{vap}}H}\, x_{\text{solute}} = \underbrace{\frac{RM\left(T_{\text{b}}^*\right)^2}{\Delta_{\text{vap}}H}}_{K_{\text{b}}}\, m.
\tag{13.22}\]

The constant \(K_{\text{b}}\) is called the ebullioscopic constant of the solvent, and it depends only on the properties of the pure solvent. For example, for water, using \(M=0.018\;\text{kg/mol}\), \(T_{\text{b}}^*=373\;\text{K}\), and \(\Delta_{\text{vap}}H=40.7\;\text{kJ/mol}\), we obtain \(K_{\text{b}}=0.51\;\frac{\text{K kg}}{\text{mol}}\), in excellent agreement with the experimental value of \(0.512\;\frac{\text{K kg}}{\text{mol}}\).
So far, we have assumed that each unit of solute produces one particle in solution. Since colligative properties depend on the number of particles, if a solute dissociates into ions, its effect is multiplied. We account for this with the van ’t Hoff factor, \(i\), which counts the number of particles produced by each formula unit of solute. The final formula for the boiling point elevation is:
\[
\Delta T_{\text{b}}=T_{\text{b}}^{\text{solution}}-T_{\text{b}}^{\text{solvent}}=iK_{\text{b}}m.
\tag{13.23}\]
For a solute that does not dissociate in solution, such as sugar, \(i=1\). For example, the strong electrolyte \(\mathrm{Ca}\mathrm{Cl}_2\) completely dissociates into three particles in solution, one \(\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}\) and two \(\mathrm{Cl}^-\), and \(i=3\). For cases of partial dissociation, such as weak acids, weak bases, and their salts, \(i\) can assume non-integer values.
The depression of the melting point is obtained with exactly the same procedure, using the equilibrium between the pure solid and the solution instead of the one between the pure vapor and the solution. The result is:
\[
\Delta T_{\text{m}}=T_{\text{m}}^{\text{solution}}-T_{\text{m}}^{\text{solvent}}=-iK_{\text{m}}m, \qquad \text{with} \qquad K_{\text{m}}=\frac{RM\left(T_{\text{m}}^*\right)^{2}}{\Delta_{\mathrm{fus}}H},
\tag{13.24}\]
where \(K_{\text{m}}\) is the cryoscopic constant of the solvent, and the minus sign accounts for the fact that the melting temperature decreases (\(\Delta T_{\text{m}}\) is negative, while \(i\), \(K_{\text{m}}\), and \(m\) are all positive). For water, \(K_{\text{m}} = 1.86\; \frac{\text{K kg}}{\text{mol}}\). This is why we spread salt on icy roads: a salt solution freezes at a lower temperature than pure water.
Notice from Figure 13.10 how the depression of the melting point is much larger than the elevation of the boiling point. To understand why, we can recall that the slope of each line in Figure 13.10 is \(-S\) (eq. 12.2). When we lower the liquid line, the new crossing point moves more if the two crossing lines have similar slopes, and less if their slopes are very different. The slopes of the liquid and the solid lines differ by the entropy of fusion, which is small, while the slopes of the liquid and gas lines differ by the entropy of vaporization, which is large. Mathematically, since \(\Delta H = T\Delta S\) at the transition, we can rewrite the two constants as \(K=RMT^*/\Delta S\), where \(\Delta S\) is the entropy of the corresponding transition. For water, \(\Delta_{\text{fus}}S=22\;\text{J}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\,\text{K}^{-1}\) and \(\Delta_{\text{vap}}S=109\;\text{J}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\,\text{K}^{-1}\), which explains why \(K_{\text{m}}\) is almost four times larger than \(K_{\text{b}}\).


13.5.3 Osmotic pressure
The osmotic pressure is probably the most important colligative property for biology and medicine. Consider the apparatus in Figure 13.11, where a solution and the pure solvent are separated by a semi-permeable (osmotic) membrane. This membrane is made of a material that lets the solvent molecules through, but blocks the solute ones.






Figure 13.11: Osmotic Pressure of a Solution.



Since the chemical potential of the solvent in the solution is lower than that of the pure solvent, eq. 13.16, the solvent spontaneously flows from the pure side into the solution, across the membrane. As a consequence, the level of the solution rises, and its pressure increases. The flow stops when the extra pressure on the solution side raises the chemical potential of its solvent back to that of the pure solvent. This extra pressure, \(\pi\), is called the osmotic pressure. We can calculate it step by step:

The equilibrium condition. At equilibrium, the chemical potential of the pure solvent at pressure \(P\) equals that of the solvent in the solution at pressure \(P+\pi\): \[
\mu_{\text{solvent}}^*(P) = \mu_{\text{solvent}}^*(P+\pi) + RT\ln x_{\text{solvent}}.
\tag{13.25}\]
The effect of pressure. As we saw in chapter 9, the chemical potential of a liquid increases with pressure as \(d\mu=\overline{V}dP\), and, since liquids are essentially incompressible, \(\mu_{\text{solvent}}^*(P+\pi)-\mu_{\text{solvent}}^*(P)=\overline{V}\pi\), where \(\overline{V}\) is the molar volume of the solvent. Replacing into eq. 13.25: \[
\overline{V}\pi = -RT\ln x_{\text{solvent}}.
\tag{13.26}\]
The dilute-solution approximation. Using again \(-\ln x_{\text{solvent}} \approx x_{\text{solute}} \approx n_{\text{solute}}/n_{\text{solvent}}\), and noticing that \(n_{\text{solvent}}\overline{V}\) is essentially the volume of the solution, \(V\): \[
\pi = \frac{n_{\text{solute}}}{V}RT = i\,cRT,
\tag{13.27}\] where \(c\) is the molar concentration of the solute, and we have introduced again the van ’t Hoff factor, \(i\), to account for dissociation.

Eq. 13.27 was proposed by van ’t Hoff, and it is remarkably similar to the ideal gas law. Morse later refined it by using the molality instead of the molar concentration, which gives better results at higher concentrations.4 Osmotic pressures can be surprisingly large: a solution with \(c=0.10\;\text{mol/L}\) of sugar at room temperature has \(\pi \approx 2.5\;\text{bar}\), enough to push a column of water up by about 25 m. This is why intravenous fluids must have the same osmotic pressure as blood: if the solution were too dilute, water would flow into the red blood cells, making them swell and burst. If we apply to the solution side a pressure higher than \(\pi\), we can reverse the flow and push pure solvent out of the solution. This process, called reverse osmosis, is widely used to obtain drinkable water from seawater.

13.6 Chapter Review

13.6.1 Practice Problems
Problem 1: Vapor Composition Above an Ideal Solution
A liquid mixture of benzene and toluene contains 40.% benzene (in moles). Calculate the total vapor pressure above the mixture at \(25\;^\circ\text{C}\), and the mole fraction of benzene in the vapor, knowing that at this temperature the vapor pressures of the pure liquids are \(P_{\text{benzene}}^*=0.127\;\text{bar}\) and \(P_{\text{toluene}}^*=0.038\;\text{bar}\). Assume that the mixture behaves as an ideal solution.
Solution: Using Raoult’s law, eq. 13.2, for each component:
\[P_{\text{benzene}} = x_{\text{benzene}} P_{\text{benzene}}^* = 0.40 \cdot 0.127\;\text{bar} = 0.0508\;\text{bar},\]
\[P_{\text{toluene}} = x_{\text{toluene}} P_{\text{toluene}}^* = 0.60 \cdot 0.038\;\text{bar} = 0.0228\;\text{bar}.\]
The total pressure is obtained from Dalton’s law:
\[P_{\text{TOT}} = 0.0508\;\text{bar} + 0.0228\;\text{bar} = 0.0736\;\text{bar},\]
and the mole fraction of benzene in the vapor is:
\[y_{\text{benzene}} = \frac{P_{\text{benzene}}}{P_{\text{TOT}}} = \frac{0.0508}{0.0736} = 0.690.\]
Answer: The total vapor pressure is \(0.074\;\text{bar}\), and the vapor contains 69% benzene (in moles), much more than the 40% in the liquid.

Problem 2: Boiling Point Elevation
Calculate the boiling point of a solution obtained by dissolving \(10.0\;\text{g}\) of glucose (\(M=180.16\;\text{g/mol}\)) in \(250.\;\text{g}\) of water at \(1\;\text{atm}\). For water, \(K_{\text{b}}=0.512\;\frac{\text{K kg}}{\text{mol}}\).
Solution: Glucose does not dissociate in water, so \(i=1\). The molality of the solution is:
\[m = \frac{n_{\text{glucose}}}{m_{\text{water}}} = \frac{10.0\;\text{g} / 180.16\;\text{g/mol}}{0.250\;\text{kg}} = \frac{0.0555\;\text{mol}}{0.250\;\text{kg}} = 0.222\;\text{mol/kg}.\]
Using eq. 13.23:
\[\Delta T_{\text{b}} = iK_{\text{b}}m = 1 \cdot 0.512\;\frac{\text{K kg}}{\text{mol}} \cdot 0.222\;\frac{\text{mol}}{\text{kg}} = 0.114\;\text{K}.\]
Answer: The solution boils at \(100.114\;^\circ\text{C}\), only about a tenth of a degree above pure water.

Problem 3: Melting Point Depression of a Salt Solution
Calculate the melting point of an aqueous solution of \(\mathrm{CaCl}_2\) with molality \(0.100\;\text{mol/kg}\). For water, \(K_{\text{m}}=1.86\;\frac{\text{K kg}}{\text{mol}}\). Assume complete dissociation.
Solution: \(\mathrm{CaCl}_2\) dissociates into one \(\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}\) and two \(\mathrm{Cl}^-\) ions, so \(i=3\). Using eq. 13.24:
\[\Delta T_{\text{m}} = -iK_{\text{m}}m = -3 \cdot 1.86\;\frac{\text{K kg}}{\text{mol}} \cdot 0.100\;\frac{\text{mol}}{\text{kg}} = -0.558\;\text{K}.\]
Answer: The solution melts at \(-0.558\;^\circ\text{C}\). Notice how the same molality of a non-dissociating solute would lower the melting point only by one third of this amount.

Problem 4: Osmotic Pressure
Calculate the osmotic pressure of an aqueous solution of sucrose with concentration \(0.0100\;\text{mol/L}\) at \(25\;^\circ\text{C}\).
Solution: Sucrose does not dissociate in water, so \(i=1\). Using eq. 13.27 with \(R=0.08314\;\frac{\text{L bar}}{\text{mol K}}\):
\[\pi = icRT = 1 \cdot 0.0100\;\frac{\text{mol}}{\text{L}} \cdot 0.08314\;\frac{\text{L bar}}{\text{mol K}} \cdot 298\;\text{K} = 0.248\;\text{bar}.\]
Answer: The osmotic pressure is \(0.248\;\text{bar}\). Even such a dilute solution pushes a column of water up by about 2.5 m.


13.6.2 Study Questions
1. What is the Gibbs phase rule for binary solutions with one phase present?

\(f = 1 - p + 2\).
\(f = 4 - p\).
\(f = 3 - p + 2\).
\(f = 3 - p\).
\(f = 2 - p + 1\).


2. Which of the following is NOT an example of a liquid solution?

Saltwater.
Vinegar.
Carbonated drinks.
Dental amalgam.
Alcoholic beverages.


3. Raoult’s law states that the partial pressure of each component \(i\) of an ideal mixture of liquids is:

\(P_i = x_i P^*_i\).
\(P_i = y_i P^*_i\).
\(P_i = \frac{x_i}{P^*_i}\).
\(P_i = x_i RT\).
\(P_i = y_i RT\).


4. In a \(T-x_B\) phase diagram of an ideal solution with two volatile components, where is the liquid phase located?

At the top of the diagram.
At the bottom of the diagram.
In the middle of the diagram.
On the left side of the diagram.
On the right side of the diagram.


5. What is an azeotrope?

A solution with a constant boiling point that cannot be altered by simple distillation.
A solution with a variable boiling point that can be easily separated by distillation.
A solution where the vapor and liquid phases have different compositions.
A solution that follows Raoult’s law perfectly.
A solution with only one volatile component.


6. How is the activity of a component in a non-ideal solution defined?

\(a_i = \gamma_i x_i\).
\(a_i = x_i\).
\(a_i = \frac{P^*_i}{P_i}\).
\(a_i = \gamma_i P_i\).
\(a_i = \frac{x_i}{P^*_i}\).


7. Which of the following is NOT a colligative property?

Vapor pressure lowering.
Boiling point elevation.
Melting point depression.
Osmotic pressure.
Molar mass.


8. Which of the following is the correct formula for boiling point elevation?

\(\Delta T_b = iK_b m\).
\(\Delta T_b = -iK_b m\).
\(\Delta T_b = \frac{iK_b}{m}\).
\(\Delta T_b = iK_b RT\).
\(\Delta T_b = iK_b P\).


9. What does the van ’t Hoff factor \(i\) in colligative property equations represent?

The number of solute particles for each formula unit.
The molality of the solution.
The molar mass of the solvent.
The vapor pressure of the solution.
The enthalpy of vaporization.


10. According to the Morse equation, the osmotic pressure \(\pi\) is given by:

\(\pi = imRT\).
\(\pi = \frac{imRT}{P}\).
\(\pi = imP\).
\(\pi = \frac{im}{RT}\).
\(\pi = imT\).








TipAnswers





1.b, 2.d, 3.a, 4.b, 5.a, 6.a, 7.e, 8.a, 9.a, 10.a

text:
Notice that, since the activity is a relative measure, the equilibrium constant expressed in terms of the activities is also a relative concept. In other words, it measures equilibrium relative to a standard state. This fact, however, should not surprise us, since the equilibrium constant is also related to \(\Delta_{\text{rxn}} G^{\standardstate}\) using Gibbs’ relation. This is why the definition of a universally agreed-upon standard state is such an essential concept in chemistry, and why it is defined by the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry (IUPAC) and followed systematically by chemists around the globe.↩︎
Molality is preferred over molarity because it does not depend on the temperature, since masses, unlike volumes, do not change when the solution is heated or cooled.↩︎
This is a plausibility argument rather than a rigorous proof, since we will use two approximations that are valid only for dilute solutions.↩︎
The Morse equation reads \(\pi = imRT\). For dilute aqueous solutions, molality and molarity are nearly equal, since 1 kg of water occupies about 1 L.↩︎

title: 14  Chemical Kinetics
text:
14.1 Differential and integrated rate laws
From thermodynamics, we can determine the spontaneity of a reaction and its extent, using \(\Delta G\) and \(K_{\text{eq}}\), respectively. However, thermodynamics does not provide any information on how fast the reaction is going to happen. For example, while the reaction that converts solid carbon from its diamond allotropic form into hexagonal graphite is thermodynamically spontaneous, it is so slow as to be virtually non-existent. Diamond is effectively a meta-stable phase. The speed of a chemical reaction is the subject of a branch of physical chemistry called chemical kinetics.
A chemical kinetics study aims to find the rate of a reaction and to find the microscopic steps that compose it, determining its mechanism.
The rate law of a chemical reaction is an equation that links the initial rate with the concentrations (or pressures) of the reactants. Rate laws usually include a constant parameter, \(k\), called the rate coefficient, and several parameters found at the exponent of the concentrations of the reactants, and are called reaction orders. The rate coefficient depends on several conditions, including the reaction type, the temperature, the surface area of an adsorbent, light irradiation, and others. The rate coefficient is usually represented with the lowercase letter \(k\), and it should not be confused with the thermodynamic equilibrium constant that is generally designated with the uppercase letter \(K\). Another useful concept in kinetics is the half-life, usually abbreviated with \(t_{1/2}\). The half-life is defined as the time required to reach half of the initial reactant concentration.
A reaction that happens in one single microscopic step is called elementary. Elementary reactions have reaction orders equal to the (integer) stoichiometric coefficients for each reactant. As such, only a limited number of elementary reactions are possible (four types are commonly observed), and they are classified according to their overall reaction order. The global reaction order of a reaction is calculated as the sum of each reactant’s individual orders and is, at most, equal to three. We examine in detail the four most common reaction orders below.
